headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: OpenHands can read/write mounted files and use MCP, while EMQX has broad network egress and HTTP API exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A direct injection bridge is plausible because OpenHands can read files, run browsers, and use MCP, while EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad egress. If EMQX outputs attacker-controlled content that OpenHands ingests as instructions, the pair can be steered. No shared channel is explicitly documented, so this is inferred and kept at medium.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied into an OpenHands task or MCP message without sanitization
IF OpenHands is configured to treat fetched HTTP content as instructions
mitigations: Require explicit provenance labels on all EMQX-derived text
Disable MCP routes that forward raw broker payloads into agent prompts
Add a short allowlist prompt template for OpenHands inputs
Use a separate workspace for fetched content and agent instructions
requires-engineering: add content-type and provenance filtering at the orchestrator boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands can read mounted files and send data to configured model providers or MCP servers; EMQX has broad network egress and touches IoT data. If both share a mounted workspace or runtime volume, sensitive files or IoT data can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs. The shared-volume path is documented for OpenHands, but EMQX’s side is inferred, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF EMQX stores IoT payloads in a directory mounted into the OpenHands runtime
IF OpenHands forwards mounted file contents to its configured model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Move EMQX data and OpenHands runtime onto separate volumes
Restrict OpenHands to a read-only mount for non-sensitive inputs
Rotate or redact IoT payloads before they enter the shared workspace
Audit outbound destinations for OpenHands model-provider calls
requires-engineering: enforce per-directory access controls in the runtime

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses inside its runtime; EMQX has broad network egress and HTTP API access. If both operate on the same mounted directory or shared mutable resource, concurrent writes or state changes can corrupt work or overwrite each other. The overlap is explicit enough to treat as dangerous by default.
conditions: IF EMQX and OpenHands share a writable mounted volume
IF OpenHands is allowed to modify git state in the same repository EMQX uses
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate writable directory
Disable git writes for OpenHands unless explicitly needed
Use file locks around any shared artifact
Run EMQX and OpenHands in separate containers with distinct mounts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can act on files and browser sessions, so if it consumes EMQX-generated text as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect edits or actions. EMQX can emit networked outputs, but there is no direct evidence that it produces facts for OpenHands by default. Because the verification gap is real, the safer medium severity is warranted.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses EMQX output as a source of truth without verification
IF EMQX output is transformed into tasks, code, or browser actions
mitigations: Require a human review step before OpenHands acts on EMQX-derived content
Add checksum or schema validation for EMQX outputs
Separate read-only analysis from write-capable execution steps
Log source-to-action mappings for later review
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating before downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while OpenHands handles files in a runtime sandbox and may send them to configured model providers. If regulated IoT or personal data is mounted into OpenHands, residency or retention obligations can diverge from EMQX’s handling. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the mismatch is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data or personal data is mounted into the OpenHands runtime
IF OpenHands model-provider calls leave the required jurisdiction or retention boundary
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the OpenHands workspace
Redact identifiers before files are mounted
Confirm model-provider region and retention settings
Document which data classes EMQX may forward
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement
